title: Tooth development & eruption dates
blurb: How teeth form, the order and ages at which deciduous and permanent teeth erupt, and why the dates matter chairside.
question: An anxious parent says their baby is 7 months old and has two bottom front teeth, but their friend's child of the same age has none yet. Later, a 7-year-old attends with new lower front teeth and a large tooth at the back of each quadrant. Are these normal, and which teeth are they?

teach.body: Deciduous teeth begin to form in the jaws at about the sixth week of pregnancy. Each tooth develops from a tooth germ that passes through stages named after its shape: bud, cap and bell. The hard tissues are then laid down, the crown is completed first, and the tooth erupts while its root is still growing. Roots are only completed in the years after eruption. Permanent teeth develop in the same way, deeper in the jaw, and the first permanent molar starts to calcify at around birth.

teach.caption: So the supporting tissues (periodontium) come from the same germ as the tooth itself.
Ages are averages. A few months either side is normal, and lower teeth usually erupt before uppers.

teach.body: From about 6 years, permanent successors push up beneath the deciduous teeth. Their pressure triggers resorption of the deciduous roots, the baby tooth loosens and is shed (exfoliated), and the permanent tooth takes its place. Shedding continues until about 12 years. At the same time, the permanent molars erupt behind the deciduous teeth without replacing anything. Eruption is often uncomfortable: teething babies may have sore, red gums, dribble more, chew things and be unsettled.

teach.h: Why the dates matter to you
teach.body: Eruption ages help the team tell deciduous from permanent teeth when charting a child, spot teeth that are late or missing, and time prevention. The first permanent molars arrive at about 6 with deep fissures, so they are the priority for fissure sealants and fluoride as soon as they erupt. Upper canines erupt late and travel a long way, so the dentist checks their position in children around 10 years old; they are one of the teeth most often impacted, after third molars.

teach.text: Deciduous order is NOT front to back. The FIRST MOLARS (about 12 months) erupt BEFORE the CANINES (about 18 months). In the permanent set the first tooth is usually the FIRST MOLAR at about 6, together with or just before the lower central incisors.

items: Tooth germs: bud, cap, bell; enamel organ → enamel, papilla → dentine and pulp, follicle → periodontium.
Deciduous: centrals ~6 months, laterals ~8, first molars ~12, canines ~18, second molars ~24; all by 2–3 years.
Permanent: first molars and lower centrals ~6 years; third molars 17–21.
Lower teeth usually erupt before uppers; upper canines are the last front teeth (11–12).

summary: You can now outline how a tooth develops, give the approximate eruption ages and order for both dentitions, explain how deciduous teeth are shed, and use eruption dates to identify teeth and time prevention such as fissure sealing first permanent molars.

A.q: Which deciduous teeth usually erupt first, at around 6 months?
A.why: The lower central incisors are usually the first teeth to appear, at around 6 months.

whyNot.0: Upper central incisors usually follow the lowers a little later.
whyNot.1: Deciduous first molars erupt at around 12 months.
whyNot.3: Deciduous canines erupt at around 18 months.

A.q: A 6-year-old attends for a check-up. Which permanent teeth are most likely to be erupting?
options: First molars and lower central incisors
Second molars and upper lateral incisors
Third molars and lower canine teeth
A.why: The first permanent molars (5–7 years) and lower central incisors (6–7 years) are the first permanent teeth to erupt.

whyNot.0: Upper canines and premolars erupt at about 10 to 12 years.
whyNot.2: Second molars erupt at about 11 to 13 years, upper laterals at 8 to 9.
whyNot.3: Third molars erupt at 17 to 21 years, lower canines at 9 to 10.

A.q: Which part of the developing tooth germ forms the cementum, periodontal ligament and alveolar bone?
A.why: The dental follicle (sac) surrounding the germ gives rise to the supporting tissues.

whyNot.0: The enamel organ forms enamel through its ameloblasts.
whyNot.1: The dental papilla forms dentine and pulp.
whyNot.2: The dental lamina is the band of tissue the tooth germs start from.

B.q: By about what age is the deciduous dentition usually complete?
B.why: The second deciduous molars erupt at around 2 years, so all 20 are usually present by about 2½ (2–3 years).

whyNot.0: At 12 months the first molars are only just arriving.
whyNot.1: At 18 months the canines are erupting and the second molars are still to come.
whyNot.3: By 5 years the deciduous set has long been complete.

B.q: In the deciduous dentition, which teeth erupt immediately before the canines?
B.why: The first molars (about 12 months) erupt before the canines (about 18 months).

whyNot.1: Second molars come last, after the canines, at about 24 months.
whyNot.2: Central incisors are the first teeth, well before the canines.
whyNot.3: Lateral incisors erupt at about 8 months, before the first molars.

B.q: What usually causes a deciduous tooth to be shed?
B.why: The erupting permanent successor triggers resorption of the deciduous root, so the tooth loosens and is exfoliated.

whyNot.0: Gum shrinkage is not the mechanism of normal shedding.
whyNot.2: Wear affects the crown but doesn't loosen the tooth.
whyNot.3: Normal shedding happens with a vital pulp; pulp death is not the trigger.

C.q: At about what age do permanent upper canines usually erupt?
C.why: Upper canines erupt at about 11 to 12 years, making them the last of the front teeth to appear.

whyNot.0: This is when the first molars and lower central incisors erupt.
whyNot.1: This is when the upper lateral incisors erupt.
whyNot.2: This is when the LOWER canines erupt; the uppers come later.

C.q: Why are first permanent molars a priority for fissure sealing soon after they erupt?
options: They are shed at about 12 years of age
They erupt at about 6 with deep fissures
They have no enamel covering the cusps
They are the last permanent teeth to erupt
C.why: They arrive at about 6 years with deep, decay-prone fissures, and must last a lifetime.

whyNot.0: First permanent molars are permanent and are not shed.
whyNot.2: Like all crowns, molar cusps are covered in enamel.
whyNot.3: Third molars, not first molars, are the last to erupt.

C.q: At what ages do third molars usually erupt, if they do?
C.why: Third molars (wisdom teeth) usually erupt between about 17 and 21 years, and are often impacted.

whyNot.0: This is when the second molars erupt.
whyNot.1: No permanent teeth normally erupt as a group at 13 to 15.
whyNot.3: Third molars usually erupt earlier than this, if they erupt at all.

reteach.title: Two queues, two rules
reteach.question: Picture the teeth waiting in two queues, one for the baby set and one for the adult set. What is the one surprise in each queue?

blocks.h: Front to back, with one jump each
blocks.body: Both queues mostly run from the front of the mouth to the back, lowers before uppers. The baby queue has one jump: the first molars push in ahead of the canines, so it goes incisors (6 to 8 months), first molars (12), canines (18), second molars (24). The adult queue has a jump right at the start: the first molars barge to the front at about 6, alongside the lower incisors. After that, front teeth (7 to 9), lower canines (9 to 10), premolars and upper canines (10 to 12), second molars (12), and third molars much later.

blocks.h: The two queues side by side

explain.body: A tooth germ passes through bud, cap and bell stages. The enamel organ forms enamel, the dental papilla forms dentine and pulp, and the dental follicle forms the cementum, PDL and bone. The crown completes before eruption; the root finishes afterwards.

test.q: Which part of the tooth germ forms dentine and pulp?
test.why: The dental papilla gives rise to the odontoblasts (which form dentine) and to the pulp.

whyNot.0: The follicle forms cementum, PDL and alveolar bone.
whyNot.3: Junctional epithelium is part of the gum attachment, not the tooth germ.

explain.body: Centrals about 6 months, laterals about 8, first molars about 12, canines about 18, second molars about 24. All 20 by about 2½ years. Lowers usually come first.

test.q: A child of 14 months has incisors and first molars but no canines yet. What is the best interpretation?
options: Normal: canines come at about 18 months
Canines are missing and need a referral
The molars have erupted too early
The canines have been shed already
test.why: Deciduous first molars (about 12 months) normally erupt before the canines (about 18 months).

whyNot.1: Canines aren't due until about 18 months, so their absence at 14 months is expected.
whyNot.2: First molars at around 12 months are on time.
whyNot.3: Deciduous canines aren't shed until about 9 to 12 years.

explain.body: First molars and lower centrals about 6; incisors 6 to 9; lower canines 9 to 10; premolars 10 to 12; upper canines 11 to 12; second molars 11 to 13; third molars 17 to 21.

explain.caption: Usually the first permanent teeth: first molars and lower central incisors.

test.q: Which permanent teeth usually erupt at around 9–10 years?
test.why: Lower canines erupt at about 9 to 10 years, earlier than the upper canines.

whyNot.0: Upper laterals erupt at about 8 to 9 years.
whyNot.1: Second molars erupt at about 11 to 13 years.
whyNot.2: Upper canines erupt later, at about 11 to 12 years.

explain.body: The permanent successor triggers resorption of the deciduous root. The tooth loosens and is exfoliated, usually between about 6 and 12 years, and the successor erupts into its place.

test.q: Over roughly which ages are deciduous teeth normally shed?
test.why: Deciduous teeth are shed during the mixed dentition, from about 6 to 12 years.

whyNot.0: At 2 to 5 years the deciduous dentition is complete and stable.
whyNot.2: By 12 to 16 most deciduous teeth have gone.
whyNot.3: This is when third molars erupt.
